title: Etale sheaves on a strictly henselian trait as specialization arrows
statement: Let $R$ be a strictly henselian discrete valuation ring [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], let $T=\operatorname{Spec}R$, let $s$ and $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}K$ be its closed and generic points, and choose a geometric generic point $\bar\eta=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ [def-weil-geometric-point]. Let $H=\operatorname{Gal}(K^{\mathrm{sep}}/K)$, where $K^{\mathrm{sep}}\subset\Omega$ is the separable closure, with its profinite topology [def-pd-separable-closure]. Let $\Lambda$ be a commutative ring. The category of sheaves of $\Lambda$-modules on $T_{\mathrm{et}}$ [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories] is equivalent to the category of triples $(W,V,a)$, where $W$ is a $\Lambda$-module with trivial $H$-action, $V$ is a discrete continuous $H$-module [def-exc-discrete-modules-category], and $a:W\to V$ is an $H$-equivariant $\Lambda$-linear map. Morphisms are pairs of linear maps commuting with $a$, with the map on $V$ $H$-equivariant. The equivalence sends $M$ to $(M_s,M_{\bar\eta},\mathrm{sp})$. Kernels and cokernels of triples are taken componentwise. Under this equivalence $\Gamma(T,M)=W$, $\Gamma(\eta,M|_\eta)=V^H$, and restriction is $a:W\to V^H$. Restriction to $\eta$ corresponds to $(W,V,a)\mapsto V$, using the equivalence between sheaves on $\eta_{\mathrm{et}}$ and discrete continuous $H$-modules.

source.place: Expose XVII, section 1.2.2 opening paragraph (printed p. 260), description by arrows; global sections at the closed point also follow from Stacks Tag 03QO, etale-cohomology.tex, lemma-vanishing-etale-cohomology-strictly-henselian

proof.text: Write $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$ and choose $\bar s$ over $s$. The residue field is separably closed. The spectrum of a DVR consists of $\eta$ and $s$: a nonzero prime ideal in a principal ideal domain is generated by an irreducible element and is maximal, and the local ring has only one maximal ideal. For a uniformizer $t$, $R[1/t]=K$, so $j:\eta\hookrightarrow T$ is the open complement of $i:s\hookrightarrow T$. Here $M_s$ denotes the geometric stalk $M_{\bar s}$, as in the source's convention; the geometric closed point is fixed throughout.

source.place: Tag 03QO, strictly henselian setup; ILO XVII section 1.2, convention ii for geometric stalk notation

proof.text: Apply [lem-exc-abelian-sheaves-gmodules] to the field $K$ and the specified algebraically closed overfield $\Omega$. This gives the equivalence on abelian sheaves with the required geometric-stalk action. It extends to every commutative coefficient ring $\Lambda$, without a finiteness assumption: an action of $\Lambda$ on an abelian sheaf is a family of additive endomorphisms $m_\lambda$, satisfying $m_1=1$, $m_{\lambda+\mu}=m_\lambda+m_\mu$ and $m_{\lambda\mu}=m_\lambda m_\mu$. Full faithfulness transports these endomorphisms and their equations in both directions. They commute with the Galois action precisely because they are morphisms in the target category. A morphism commutes with every $m_\lambda$ precisely when it is linear. Actions by the constant ring sheaf are equivalent to these actions by constant scalars: locally a section of the constant ring sheaf is represented by a constant scalar, and its action is then defined locally and glued uniquely. Thus the resulting equivalence $E_\eta$ sends module sheaves to discrete continuous $H$-modules. Denote its inverse at $V$ by $F_V$.

source.place: Tag 04JQ, lemma-equivalence-abelian-sheaves-point; scalar-endomorphism transport and sheafification of constant scalars

proof.text: Apply the same abelian-sheaf equivalence to the separably closed field $\kappa$ and extend scalars exactly as in Step 2. Its absolute Galois group is trivial, so this gives an equivalence $E_s:\operatorname{Mod}(s_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)\simeq\operatorname{Mod}_\Lambda$ whose functor is the closed geometric stalk. Write $C(W)$ for its inverse. In particular maps $C(W)\to C(A)$ are exactly linear maps $W\to A$, and every sheaf on $s_{\mathrm{et}}$ is determined, including its morphisms, by its stalk. The functors $i^{-1},j^{-1}$ and their right adjoints are module functors for this same constant ring by [prop-weil-pbc-inverse-image-modules-exact].

source.place: Tag 04JQ with trivial absolute Galois group; Tag 03Q1, lemma-stalk-pullback, and constant-coefficient inverse image

proof.text: For a module sheaf $F$ on $\eta$, put $V=E_\eta(F)$ and $B=i^{-1}j_*F$. Its sections satisfy $F(\eta)=\operatorname{Hom}(\underline{\mathbf Z}_\eta,F)$ as abelian groups: a map is sent to the image of the global constant section $1$, and a section defines the inverse map on constant integers by multiplication, extended uniquely to the constant sheaf. By [lem-weil-pbc-constant-sheaf-geometric-stalk], the canonical stalk of this constant sheaf is $\mathbf Z$; its Galois action is trivial since changing a pointed lift leaves every constant germ unchanged. Full faithfulness of [lem-exc-abelian-sheaves-gmodules] therefore identifies these maps with $\operatorname{Hom}_H(\mathbf Z,V)=V^H$, by evaluation at $1$. This comparison is exactly the generic germ map and is linear for $\Lambda$, since taking the germ commutes with each scalar. It applies to the arbitrary algebraically closed overfield $\Omega$ in that equivalence. Next [lem-weil-pbc-strictly-henselian-sections-stalk] and the direct-image formula give $(j_*F)_{\bar s}=\Gamma(T,j_*F)=F(\eta)=V^H$. By [lemma-openclosed-stalk-upperstar], $E_s(B)=(j_*F)_{\bar s}$, so Step 3 identifies $B$ naturally with $C(V^H)$. These identifications describe the actual germ maps.

Define $\Phi(M)$ by $W=M_{\bar s}$, $V=E_\eta(j^{-1}M)$ and the composite $W\simeq M(T)\to(j^{-1}M)(\eta)\simeq V^H\hookrightarrow V$. Here the first isomorphism is the inverse of the germ isomorphism of [lem-weil-pbc-strictly-henselian-sections-stalk], and the second is Step 4's invariant-sections comparison. This is the specialization map: represent the closed germ by its global section on $T$ and restrict that section to the fixed geometric generic point. Its image is invariant, so the map is equivariant when $W$ has trivial action. By [lemma-openclosed-stalk-upperstar] applied to $j$, $V=(j^{-1}M)_{\bar\eta}\cong M_{j\circ\bar\eta}$ naturally in $M$, so $V$ is the generic geometric stalk $M_{\bar\eta}$ of the statement, and the composite is the germ at $\bar\eta$ of the global representative. Every sheaf morphism gives a pair of linear stalk maps, the generic map equivariant, and naturality of restriction makes their square commute. This defines a functor to the stated category of triples.

source.place: ILO XVII section 1.2.2 opening paragraph, arrow of stalks; Tags 03QO and 03QW

proof.text:
Given a triple $(W,V,a)$, factor $a$ uniquely through $b:W\to V^H$; this uses exactly its equivariance and the trivial action on $W$. Take $F=F_V$ from Step 2 and $B=i^{-1}j_*F\simeq C(V^H)$ from Step 4. Through the fully faithful functor $E_s$, $b$ gives a map $\beta:C(W)\to B$. Define
$$\Psi(W,V,a)=j_*F\mathbin{\times}_{i_*B}i_*C(W),$$
where the first map to $i_*B$ is the unit $q:j_*F\to i_*i^{-1}j_*F$ and the second is $i_*\beta$. This fiber product exists explicitly: on each etale object take pairs of sections having equal images; compatible pairs glue uniquely because each factor is a sheaf. Scalar operations are componentwise. These sectionwise submodules define its universal property by projection. A commuting pair of triple maps gives the maps of $F$, $B$ and $C(W)$, hence a map of these fiber products. Identity and composition hold on both projections, defining $\Psi$.

source.place: Tag 03Q1, inverse-image/direct-image adjunction; explicit fiber-product construction expanding ILO XVII section 1.2.2

proof.text:
Compute the two restrictions of this fiber product. By [prop-weil-pbc-inverse-image-modules-exact], inverse image preserves it. The fully faithful closed direct image of [lem-kun-04ca] has counit $i^{-1}i_*\simeq1$ and has zero restriction to $\eta$; these facts pass to module sheaves because the counit commutes with every scalar. Similarly [lem-sc-open-immersion-pushforward-fully-faithful] gives $j^{-1}j_*F\simeq F$. On applying $i^{-1}$ to $q$, the triangle identity identifies the map $B\to i^{-1}i_*B\simeq B$ with the identity. Consequently
$$i^{-1}\Psi\simeq B\times_B C(W)\simeq C(W),\qquad j^{-1}\Psi\simeq F\times_0 0\simeq F.$$
Under these identifications the closed stalk of the first projection $\Psi\to j_*F$ is $b$. By naturality of the germ comparison in Step 4, the restriction of global sections is therefore $b$, and the specialization map is $a$. All comparisons commute with triple morphisms, yielding $\Phi\Psi\simeq1$.

For $M$, put $F=j^{-1}M$ and $A=i^{-1}M$. Its units give maps $M\to j_*F$ and $M\to i_*A$. The map $A\to B=i^{-1}j_*F$ is $i^{-1}$ of the first unit. Naturality of the $i$-unit makes the two composites $M\to i_*B$ equal. Step 4 and naturality of the closed germ identify $A\simeq C(W)$ and this map $A\to B$ with the map $b$ used by $\Psi\Phi$. Thus the pair gives a natural map $r_M:M\to\Psi\Phi(M)$. On $i^{-1}$ and $j^{-1}$, the triangle identities and the fiber-product descriptions of Step 7 identify $r_M$ with the identity of $A$ and $F$, respectively. By [lemma-openclosed-stalk-upperstar], its maps at $\bar s$ and $\bar\eta$ are therefore isomorphisms. These two geometric points cover $T$ by Step 1; [lem-weil-pbc-sets-etale-iso-on-geometric-stalks] makes the underlying set-sheaf map an isomorphism. The inverse commutes with addition and scalars by composing its defining inverse identities with those operations. Hence $r_M$ is a module-sheaf isomorphism and $\Psi\Phi\simeq1$. Together with Step 7 this proves the claimed equivalence, with exactly the specified stalk functor and morphisms.

source.place: Tags 03Q1, lemma-stalk-pullback; 03PU, theorem-exactness-stalks; explicit units and fiber-product universal property

proof.text: For a morphism of triples $(f,g):(W,V,a)\to(W',V',a')$, its kernel is $(\ker f,\ker g,a|_{\ker f})$, since $ga=a'f$ sends $\ker f$ into $\ker g$. Its cokernel is $(W'/f(W),V'/g(V),\bar a')$, where $\bar a'([w'])=[a'(w')]$; this is well defined because $a'f=ga$. Both arrows remain equivariant, and the maps on the closed modules still have trivial action. The kernel action is continuous by restriction; on the quotient the stabilizer of $[v']$ contains the open stabilizer of $v'$, so the quotient action is continuous as well. For any triple map killed by $(f,g)$, its two component maps factor uniquely through the two kernels, and their compatibility follows by the inclusions; dually a triple map killing $(f,g)$ factors uniquely through the two quotients, and compatibility follows by the surjections. These are precisely the kernel and cokernel universal properties. Thus the asserted componentwise description holds, and the equivalence transports the corresponding kernels and cokernels of sheaves.

source.place: ILO XVII section 1.2.2, module arrows; componentwise kernel and cokernel universal properties

proof.text: Finally [lem-weil-pbc-strictly-henselian-sections-stalk] identifies $\Gamma(T,M)$ naturally with $W$, while Step 4 identifies $\Gamma(\eta,j^{-1}M)$ with $V^H$. The definition of $\Phi$ in Step 5 says their restriction is $b:W\to V^H$, namely $a$ with codomain its invariant submodule. Also its generic component is exactly $E_\eta(j^{-1}M)$, so restriction to $\eta$ is the forgetful functor $(W,V,a)\mapsto V$ under $E_\eta$. This establishes all the functor and sections clauses.
